name: Richardsonian Romanesque

lineage.note: The round arch, the squat column, and the massive wall are quoted; Richardson's own sources were closer to Auvergne, Provence, and Salamanca than to England, and none of them transmitted building practice to him.

Real transmission. Richardson was the second American to study at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts, and the plan discipline, the parti, and the compositional hierarchy of his buildings are Beaux-Arts training applied to Romanesque forms.
Against thin, brittle, applied eclecticism and the mansarded pile, in favour of mass, weight, continuity, and material presence.
Specifically against High Victorian polychromy and linear ornament; Richardson replaced pattern with mass.

description.short: H. H. Richardson's personal manner and its national imitation: rock-faced ashlar, deep round arches springing from squat columns or from the ground, and a wall so heavy and continuous that the building reads as a single geological mass.
description.long:
This is the only American style named for a person, and the attribution is honest, because the style is one man's solution and everything after Trinity Church in Boston, won in competition in 1872 and finished in 1877, is imitation of varying quality. Henry Hobson Richardson trained at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris in the 1860s, and what he brought back was not a vocabulary but a method: establish the parti, subordinate everything to a single dominant idea, and make the building one thing. He then took a vocabulary, southern French and Spanish Romanesque, that nobody in America had a claim on, and used it to make masses instead of pictures. His imitators took the vocabulary and mostly missed the method, which is why there are ten thousand rock-faced arches in America and perhaps forty buildings that work.

The style stands at an unusual angle to the technological rupture that organises this branch. Everything else here rides cheap light framing and cheap machine ornament; Richardsonian Romanesque insists on load-bearing masonry at exactly the moment American construction was abandoning it. Its own enabling technologies are different ones: mechanised quarrying and the pneumatic and steam stone saw, which made large rock-faced blocks of granite, sandstone, and brownstone economically shippable, and the transcontinental railroad that moved them. There is also a labour story. The style depends on the presence of skilled stonecutters, many of them recent Scottish, Irish, Italian, and German immigrants, in American cities in the 1880s, and it dies in the 1890s partly because steel frame construction made the load-bearing masonry wall obsolete for tall buildings and partly because those crews and their wage rates could not be sustained.

What it rejected was the entire Victorian assumption that a building should be interesting all over. Richardson's walls are large, quiet, and mostly blank; his openings are few, deep, and grouped; his ornament is concentrated in narrow bands of carved foliage at a capital or a string course and is otherwise absent. The effect is a hierarchy of attention that no other Victorian style attempts. He is also the only architect of the period whose buildings improve as you approach: from across the street you read one mass and one arch, from the sidewalk you read the coursing and the tooling of the stone, and at the door you find the carving, which is worked at exactly the scale of a hand.

In front of one, the dominant sensation is compression and weight. The entrance arch springs from near the ground or from columns so short and thick that they read as pressed down by the wall above; the voussoirs are large enough to count; the wall recedes into a deep reveal so that entering is genuinely a passage through thickness rather than through a plane. Inside a Richardson house the surprise is warmth: heavy oak, inglenooks, low broad openings, and rooms that are dark at the perimeter and bright at the windows, which are always fewer and larger than you expect. It is the only Victorian style that feels like shelter rather than display.

defining_characteristics: Load-bearing masonry construction, in rock-faced squared ashlar of granite, sandstone, or brownstone
Deep semicircular arches at the principal entrance, springing from short heavy columns or directly from a plinth or the ground
Massive continuous wall surface with a low proportion of opening, and windows deeply recessed in the wall thickness
Broad simple roof forms, low hipped or with a few large gables, subordinate to the wall mass
Towers that are round, squat, and conically capped, engaged with the mass rather than attached to it
Ornament confined to narrow bands of carved Byzantine or Romanesque foliage at capitals, string courses, and the entrance arch
Polychromy by stone selection and coursing, never by paint or applied pattern
diagnostic_tells: The arch springs from the ground or from a column no more than three diameters tall; a tall slender column under a round arch indicates a later commercial imitation
Rock-faced stone with quarry tooling left visible, laid in broken-range or random coursing, with the face projecting 2 to 4 in beyond the joint
Window openings grouped in bands of three or five under a single relieving arch or lintel, rather than distributed one per bay
The tower, if any, is round and squat with a conical cap and is engaged into the corner of the mass; a slender detached tower is a different style
Compared with Queen Anne: no texture change, no applied ornament, no porch. The wall is one material top to bottom

distinguished_from.difference: Contemporary and often on the same street, but opposite in every value: mass versus articulation, one material versus many textures, few large openings versus many small ones, load-bearing stone versus balloon frame.

Shares Richardson himself and shares the doctrine of continuous unbroken surface, which is precisely why the two are linked in the graph. The difference is material and weight: shingle is a taut light skin over a wooden volume, ashlar is the mass itself.

The quoted source. English Norman work is genuinely twelfth-century, thin-jointed, with cushion capitals and chevron ornament and a real structural logic of pier and vault; the Richardsonian arch is a nineteenth-century masonry veneer of feeling with a steel or timber floor system behind it in all but the largest examples.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Governed by mass and by the arch. The entrance arch is the module of feeling for the whole building: its span sets the wall's apparent thickness, the coursing scale, and the depth of every reveal. Beaux-Arts parti discipline organises the plan beneath it.
typical_ratios: Wall opening area 20 to 35 percent of any elevation; the wall must win
Entrance arch span 8 to 16 ft, with voussoir depth 1/8 to 1/6 of the span
Column height 2 to 3.5 shaft diameters where columns are used at all
Ashlar course height 8 to 14 in, face projection 2 to 4 in beyond the joint plane
Tower diameter 12 to 20 ft, height to eave 1.2 to 1.8 times diameter
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Grouped and hierarchical rather than repetitive: a large arched opening, a band of three or five smaller openings, and long stretches of blank wall. The rhythm is A - BBB - A, not A-A-A-A.

massing_affinities.note: Picturesque in outline but massive in substance, which is the style's particular achievement.
The rock-faced brownstone row of Boston, Chicago, and Denver.
A mansard converts mass into crown and destroys the continuity the style depends on.

constraints.statement: Exterior walls shall be load-bearing masonry of not less than 16 in nominal thickness at the ground storey, with window reveals of 12 to 24 in. Thin stone veneer over a frame wall is prohibited; the style is entirely an argument about wall thickness.

test.note: Tests the wall-thickness minimum, the clause the statement itself calls the governing one ('the style is entirely an argument about wall thickness'). The paired window-reveal range (12-24 in, reveal_depth_in) is a second numeric fact the schema's single test object can't also carry, and stays prose alongside the thin-veneer-over-frame prohibition.

constraints.statement: Principal arches shall be semicircular. Pointed, segmental, and elliptical arches are forbidden at the entrance. Where columns support an arch, shaft height shall not exceed 3.5 base diameters.
Openings shall occupy not more than 35 percent of the area of any elevation, and shall be grouped rather than evenly distributed.

test.note: Tests the opening-area ceiling. 'Grouped rather than evenly distributed' is a spatial-distribution fact with no matching vocabulary variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: One wall material shall run from water table to eave on every elevation. Texture, colour, and coursing may vary within the material; a change of material at a storey line is prohibited.
Carved ornament shall be confined to capitals, the entrance arch, and not more than two continuous bands per elevation, and shall total not more than 8 percent of the elevation area.

exemplars.name: Trinity Church
exemplars.note: H. H. Richardson, competition won 1872, dedicated 1877. The building that established the manner and made Richardson the most imitated architect in America.

exemplars.name: John J. Glessner House
exemplars.note: H. H. Richardson, designed 1885, completed 1887. Granite street walls turned almost blank to the corner with the rooms opening to a private south courtyard; the definitive domestic statement of the style.

exemplars.name: Allegheny County Courthouse and Jail
exemplars.note: H. H. Richardson, 1884-88, completed after his death in 1886. Richardson himself considered it his best work.

sources: Jeffrey Karl Ochsner, H. H. Richardson: Complete Architectural Works (1982)
Henry-Russell Hitchcock, The Architecture of H. H. Richardson and His Times (1936; rev. 1961)
James F. O'Gorman, Three American Architects: Richardson, Sullivan and Wright, 1865-1915 (1991)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)

proportion_packs.note: Bound with a caution its own record supplies. The pack takes one figure from here and it is the only one of its kind in the corpus -- 'voussoir depth 1/8 to 1/6 of the span' -- which governs archivolt depth for every node the pack binds. What sits OUTSIDE the pack's band deliberately is this node's own signature: an 'entrance arch span 8 to 16 ft', which is one great arch used as an event and not a rhythm, and which this pack's span rule explicitly declines to proportion. Use the voussoir rule here and the bay rules only where there is a genuine arcade rather than a single arch.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to, but its governing role is narrower here than on the wooden Victorian styles: the node's own proportional_system says the elevation is 'governed by mass and by the arch,' with hierarchy made by grouped-vs-blank wall (A-BBB-A) rather than by the pack's dominant-mass-vs-subordinate-mass logic in the usual sense. What transfers cleanly is the datum discipline (the pack's continuous-horizontal rule, which matches this node's wall material running unbroken water-table to eave) and the one-feature-window logic. The dominance ratio and wing-strategy rules are a poor fit for a single-block masonry mass and should be read loosely if at all.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to. Governs the ashlar coursing scale (8-14 in course height per the node vs. the pack's whole-course arithmetic), the water table, and the general discipline that every horizontal is a whole number of courses off one datum — genuinely applicable to load-bearing stone as well as brick, since the pack's coursing logic is generic to coursed masonry. It does NOT cover the style's defining semicircular entrance arch: brick-course's arch rules are segmental and flat-jack-arch derivations, and this node requires full semicircular arches (c02) springing from squat columns, which is a real gap — see report.

JUDGMENT BINDING. Not in this pack's applies_to. Bound low and secondary because the style's few, deeply recessed, grouped windows (20-35 percent opening area) are still real double-hung sash of the 1872-1905 period and would carry the same late-cylinder/plate-glass light counts as the rest of the corpus's Victorian nodes; but the pack's window-head and casing rules are calibrated to wood-frame construction and are secondary here to brick-course's masonry-specific window_head_masonry rule for the actual opening geometry.

JUDGMENT BINDING. Not in this pack's applies_to. Bound over room-vernacular because the node explicitly credits 'Beaux-Arts parti discipline' organizing the plan beneath the Romanesque forms, and Richardson is documented as the second American to study at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts — a formally trained, hierarchically composed plan is closer to this pack's rank-and-suite logic (adjacent rooms differing by one term of the series, breadth held constant across a suite) than to room-vernacular's structurally-constrained folk room. No specific source ties Richardson's own room dimensions to Palladio's ratios, and this binding should be read as 'the closest available system for a formally planned room,' not as a documented fact about Richardson's practice.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own notes make its subject a composition in vertical strips, and its composition_parti rule states the travee is "16 ft on centre and UNIFORM ALONG A RANGE" -- "a French range does not graduate its bays or widen a centre one, it repeats a strip" -- while its dormer rules put exactly one lucarne per travee at 0.6 to 0.9 of the bay's width. The node's bay_rhythm refuses that repetition in the same terms the pack asserts it, and its tell places windows "grouped in bands of three or five under a single relieving arch or lintel, rather than distributed one per bay", so there is no one-opening-per-bay axis for a strip to stand on or a lucarne to cap. The massing record adds that mansard-block is forbidden because "A mansard converts mass into crown and destroys the continuity the style depends on", which is the pack's third item. This is a contradiction of the pack's stated mechanism, not merely of its figures.
declined_packs.quote: The rhythm is A - BBB - A, not A-A-A-A.
declined_packs.note: governs 2 slots; declining loses no dimensioning at all -- composition_parti passes to facade-peristyle (roman-classical) and dormer to storey-graduation (beaux-arts-french); 0 slots lose all dimensioning.
